title: The 'text/html' Media Type
summary: Summarizes the history of HTML development and defines the text/html media type by pointing to the relevant W3C recommendations. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: This gives the web page format its official label, so computers know a file is a web page when they receive it.

questions: what is the html mime type
what is the text/html media type
what is the charset parameter in text/html
subtitle: The registration that makes text/html the official label for web pages, and hands the definition of HTML over to the W3C.

tldr.problem: HTML had been defined by several IETF documents and many informal extensions, and the work of defining it had moved to the W3C, so the IETF record was out of date.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2854 registers the text/html MIME media type, points to the W3C Recommendations as the definition of HTML, and obsoletes the earlier IETF HTML documents.
tldr.outcome: HTML leaves the IETF Standards Track. The RFC is Informational and stays as the registration of the text/html type, with notes on charset, line breaks, fragment identifiers and recognizing HTML files.

today: RFC 2854 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 1866, RFC 1867, RFC 1980, RFC 1942 and RFC 2070.

sections.title: How HTML Got Here
sections.content:
The RFC opens with a short history. HTML has been in use in the World Wide Web since 1990 and was specified in various informal documents. The text/html media type was first officially defined by the IETF HTML working group in 1995. Extensions were proposed in separate documents for HTML 3.0, file upload, tables, client-side image maps and internationalization.

The IETF HTML working group closed in September 1996, and the work moved to the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). The extensions were folded in to some extent in HTML 3.2 and to a larger extent in HTML 4.0. The RFC also notes a reformulation of HTML 4.0 in XML 1.0 and the wide variety of extensions popularized by Mosaic, Netscape Navigator and Microsoft Internet Explorer.

Its stated aim is to obsolete RFC 1866, RFC 1867, RFC 1980, RFC 1942 and RFC 2070, and to remove HTML from the IETF Standards Track.
sections.eli5: The rules for web pages were first written by one group of people and then passed to another group. This note says so, and retires the old rule books.

sections.title: The text/html Registration
sections.content:
Section 2 is the formal MIME registration form. The type is text, the subtype is html, and there are no required parameters. The one optional parameter is charset, which names the character encoding of the document. Any registered IANA charset may be used, UTF-8 is preferred, and the RFC strongly recommends always including it. The old level and version parameters were never used in practice and are removed.

The definition itself is not in this RFC. It says the media type is now defined by W3C Recommendations, with HTML 4.01 as the latest version at the time, and that XHTML 1.0 may also be labeled text/html. The W3C has change control over the HTML specification.

The form also warns that implementers of text/html interpreters must be prepared to be bug-compatible with popular browsers, because many HTML variants are in use. Versions are usually told apart by the DOCTYPE declaration, though it is sometimes omitted or wrong. There is no single magic number, and file extensions html and htm are common.
sections.eli5: Filling in the official form for the name tag: the kind is text, the type is html, and you can add a note saying which alphabet it uses. The rule book for what is inside lives with the W3C.

sections.title: Fragments, Encoding and Charset
sections.content:
For documents labeled text/html, a fragment identifier (the part of a URI after the hash sign) designates the element with that name. Any element may be named with the id attribute, and the A, APPLET, FRAME, IFRAME, IMG and MAP elements may also be named with a name attribute.

Because HTML has character entity references, a document with a wide range of characters can still be written in US-ASCII and sent without extra encoding. Other charsets may need base64 or quoted-printable on 7-bit channels. As with all MIME text subtypes, the canonical form uses a CR byte (0x0D) followed by an LF byte (0x0A) for every line break, and CR or LF outside such a sequence is forbidden. HTTP allows other end-of-line conventions, and that exception is commonly used for HTML.

On charset defaults, MIME says US-ASCII and HTTP says ISO-8859-1 for text subtypes, but the RFC notes that the overwhelming majority of deployed browsers use something else. An explicit charset parameter avoids the confusion.
sections.eli5: Always write on the page which alphabet you used, because the computers receiving it may otherwise guess differently. Each line must end with the agreed line-ending marker.

sections.title: Recognizing HTML Files
sections.content:
Almost all HTML files have the string <html or <HTML near the beginning. Documents conforming to HTML 2.0, 3.2 and 4.0 start with a <!DOCTYPE HTML declaration before the <html, and these dialects are case insensitive. Files may start with white space, comments or processing instructions before the DOCTYPE.

XHTML documents optionally start with an XML declaration beginning <?xml and are required to have a <!DOCTYPE html declaration.
sections.eli5: Most web pages begin with a little sign that says html. Looking for that sign is how a program can tell it is holding a web page.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to HTML 4.01, section B.10, which notes various security issues with interpreting anchors and forms. It adds that scripting languages and interactive features introduced in HTML 4.0 bring risks from the automatic execution of programs written by the sender but run by the recipient.

User agents that execute such scripts or programs must be extremely careful to make sure that untrusted software runs in a protected environment.
sections.eli5: A web page can carry little programs. Your browser must run them in a safe box in case a stranger wrote something nasty.
